biz-b1-delegate-first-task.q: You're choosing your first task to delegate to AI. Which criterion set does the lesson say to prioritize?
options: A task with a clear right answer, a fast check, and real time cost — not the hardest or most important task
The most important, highest-stakes task you can think of
A task that requires your personal judgment or a specific relationship
Whatever task takes the least time to describe
biz-b1-delegate-first-task.why: The lesson recommends picking the first delegation based on a clear right answer, fast checkability, and real time cost, not the hardest task you can think of.

biz-b1-delegate-first-task.q: The prompt instructs: if something needed to do the task well is missing from the source material, list it under 'Questions before I finalize this' instead of guessing. Why does this matter?
options: It makes the output shorter
It stops a task with gaps from turning into a confident-sounding draft with invented details
It's required for the AI to process the source material
It guarantees the draft will be approved without edits
biz-b1-delegate-first-task.why: This rule keeps a task with missing information from becoming a confident-sounding draft with invented facts — you get an honest list of gaps instead.

biz-b1-delegate-first-task.q: After delegating a task and getting a draft back, what should you do before using it?
options: Paste it straight into the client-facing document since it already matches your brief
Immediately ask for a completely different task
Check that every fact traces to the source material, the format is right, and nothing is invented
Judge the tool as reliable after one good result without further checks
biz-b1-delegate-first-task.why: The lesson's check step requires verifying facts trace to the source, the format is correct, and nothing was invented, before the draft is used.

biz-b2-customer-communication.q: You're drafting a reply to a customer complaint. According to the lesson, what's the biggest actual risk of using AI here?
options: The grammar will be poor
The AI will refuse to draft anything about complaints
The message will be too short
The draft might promise something (a discount, timeline, exception) you didn't actually authorize
biz-b2-customer-communication.why: The real risk isn't wording quality — it's AI being generous with your business on your behalf by promising a commitment you never actually decided on.

biz-b2-customer-communication.q: Why does the prompt ban generic corporate phrases like 'we take this very seriously' unless you've used them yourself?
options: It keeps the message sounding like you instead of a template, which matters most when a customer is already frustrated
Those phrases are considered legal admissions of fault
They make the message too long
AI tools are incapable of generating them accurately
biz-b2-customer-communication.why: Banning generic corporate phrases by default keeps the message sounding like you, which matters most exactly when a customer is already upset.

biz-b2-customer-communication.q: Before sending a difficult-message draft, what should you specifically re-read it for?
options: Spelling errors only
Overcommitment — anything promised that wasn't in your stated facts — and a defensive or over-apologetic tone
Whether it's long enough
Whether it uses your brand's logo colors
biz-b2-customer-communication.why: The lesson's check step specifically calls for reading once for overcommitment and once for tone against the situation.

biz-i1-market-competitor-research-perple.q: Why is Gemini's Deep Research well-suited to competitor/market research compared to a general chat model?
options: It's free to use unlike other tools
It only searches your own uploaded documents
It runs a multi-step research plan across live sources and answers with cited, dated results, letting you verify claims instead of trusting an unverifiable paragraph
It doesn't require an account
biz-i1-market-competitor-research-perple.why: Deep Research answers with sources by default, giving you a citation trail you can defend to a partner or lender, unlike a confident-sounding paragraph you can't verify.

biz-i1-market-competitor-research-perple.q: The prompt asks Gemini to flag if it had to widen the search beyond your specified region or segment. What problem does this prevent?
options: Running out of search credits
The report being too short
Citing too many sources
Unknowingly treating a broad national trend as if it were specific evidence about your local market
biz-i1-market-competitor-research-perple.why: This instruction stops you from unknowingly treating broader, widened-search data as if it were specific to your exact market.

biz-i1-market-competitor-research-perple.q: What should you do with the cited sources before using a figure in a real business decision?
options: Open at least two or three yourself and confirm they're recent and specific to your market
Trust the summary paragraph without opening any citations
Only check citations older than 12 months
Ignore citations entirely since Deep Research verifies them for you
biz-i1-market-competitor-research-perple.why: The lesson explicitly recommends personally opening several citations to confirm they're recent and actually relevant before relying on a figure.

biz-i2-standard-operating-procedures.q: You're turning a task into an SOP. What should you feed the AI as the raw input?
options: A generic industry-standard version of the task
Your actual messy walkthrough of the task, including exceptions and judgment calls, not a cleaned-up version
Only the ideal-case steps, skipping exceptions
A list of tools you use, without describing the steps
biz-i2-standard-operating-procedures.why: Starting from a raw, unedited walkthrough is what captures the exceptions and judgment calls that make a task hard to hand off, which a tidy description misses.

biz-i2-standard-operating-procedures.q: Why does the prompt instruct the AI to flag gaps as '[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]' instead of filling them in with a plausible-sounding step?
options: It makes the SOP look more professional
Clarification tags are required by SOP software
A wrong invented step is worse than a missing one — someone will follow it confidently and get it wrong
It shortens the document
biz-i2-standard-operating-procedures.why: Flagging gaps instead of inventing steps matters because a confidently wrong invented step in an SOP is worse than an honestly flagged gap.

biz-i2-standard-operating-procedures.q: After drafting the SOP, what's the recommended way to validate it?
options: Assume it's clear because you, the author, understand it
Publish it immediately without testing
Have the same person who wrote the walkthrough review it alone
Have a teammate attempt the task using only the document while you observe where they get stuck, then revise based on that
biz-i2-standard-operating-procedures.why: The lesson recommends a real test run with a teammate, revising the SOP based specifically on where they hesitated or asked a question.

biz-i3-financial-narratives.q: Your P&L shows margin dropped two points. The AI drafts: 'this is likely due to a pricing change.' You never told it about a pricing change. What should you do?
options: Flag and remove it — the rule against inventing a business reason means it should only describe what the numbers show or use context you actually gave it
Keep it since it's a plausible-sounding explanation
Ask the AI to make the explanation more specific
Move it into the confirmed changes section
biz-i3-financial-narratives.why: The prompt's core rule bans inventing a business reason for a change unless it's stated in the data or you supplied it, so an unverified guess should be removed.

biz-i3-financial-narratives.q: Why does the prompt include a section titled 'Changes I can't explain from the numbers alone'?
options: It's required financial reporting terminology
It separates confirmed changes from unexplained ones, turning the exercise into useful pre-meeting prep instead of a source of confidently wrong talking points
It makes the report look more thorough for investors
It replaces the need to talk to a bookkeeper entirely
biz-i3-financial-narratives.why: This section keeps confirmed changes separate from unexplained ones, which is what makes the exercise useful rather than a source of confidently wrong talking points.

biz-i3-financial-narratives.q: Before pasting a financial export into a general consumer AI account, what does the lesson recommend?
options: Nothing — general accounts are always safe for financial data
Convert all numbers to percentages first
Redact or generalize sensitive details like customer names or account numbers first, or use business-tier data settings
Only paste data older than one year
biz-i3-financial-narratives.why: The lesson recommends redacting sensitive details or using business-tier data settings before pasting financial exports into a general AI account.

biz-a1-ai-operations-layer.q: You're designing an automation that emails customers about order delays. According to the lesson, what must the first version include?
options: Full autonomy from day one, to prove the system works
No fallback plan, since AI rarely fails
A cheaper AI model to reduce cost
An explicit human-approval checkpoint before anything external (sending, spending) happens, since it's customer-facing
biz-a1-ai-operations-layer.why: The lesson requires a human checkpoint on anything external, like customer-facing sends, and warns against automating this with no checkpoint on the first version.

biz-a1-ai-operations-layer.q: Why does the workflow spec separate 'mechanical' steps from steps needing 'AI judgment'?
options: Mechanical steps should go to a simpler MCP connector or scheduled action, reserving AI for genuine judgment, which keeps the system simpler and cheaper to run
AI can't perform mechanical steps at all
It's required by Claude's and ChatGPT's pricing tiers
Mechanical steps always need more approval
biz-a1-ai-operations-layer.why: Separating mechanical from AI-judgment steps keeps the system simpler and cheaper by reserving AI for genuine judgment tasks only.

biz-a1-ai-operations-layer.q: What is one of the most common ways these automations quietly go wrong, according to the lesson?
options: The workflow runs too infrequently
The workflow has no assigned owner responsible for periodically checking its output
Too many human checkpoints slow it down
The trigger event is too specific
biz-a1-ai-operations-layer.why: An automation with no owner is called out as the most common way these workflows quietly go wrong, since no one notices a silent failure.

fl-b1-proposals-that-win.q: Why does the prompt require pasting the client's brief verbatim rather than your summary of it?
options: Verbatim text is required for copyright reasons
Summaries take longer to process
It lets the model mirror the client's own language back, which reads as far more tailored than generic industry terms
It reduces the total word count of the proposal
fl-b1-proposals-that-win.why: Feeding in the brief verbatim lets the model mirror the client's own wording, and proposals that echo a client's specific language read as far more tailored.

fl-b1-proposals-that-win.q: The prompt blocks the AI from filling in a specific price, timeline, or scope. Why?
options: Clients prefer proposals without any numbers
It's illegal to state a price in a first draft
It makes the proposal shorter
Those are business decisions you should make deliberately, not accept because a plausible number appeared in a first draft
fl-b1-proposals-that-win.why: Blocking price, timeline, and scope from the draft is deliberate, since those are decisions you should make yourself rather than accept from a plausible-sounding draft.

fl-b1-proposals-that-win.q: Which of these is a mistake the lesson warns against?
options: Letting the draft list every skill you have instead of the 2-3 that match this specific brief
Reading the brief yourself first to note the client's top priorities
Pulling 2-4 real proof points from past work
Editing the opening line by hand
fl-b1-proposals-that-win.why: The lesson lists listing every skill instead of the 2-3 that match the specific brief as a common mistake that makes a proposal read as generic.

fl-b2-client-onboarding-docs.q: Why does the prompt ask you to list your actual requirements and week-one commitments instead of asking for generic onboarding advice?
options: Generic advice is against platform policy
It produces a packet clients can follow without emailing back to ask what you meant, unlike generic advice
It's faster to generate generic advice
Clients prefer longer documents
fl-b2-client-onboarding-docs.why: Feeding in your real requirements and commitments, instead of generic advice, is what makes the packet something clients can actually follow without follow-up questions.

fl-b2-client-onboarding-docs.q: What's the benefit of building the kickoff email as a template with bracketed placeholders?
options: Placeholders are required by email clients
It makes the email look more formal
It saves real time on the next client, not just this one, instead of rewriting the whole document each time
It prevents the client from replying directly
fl-b2-client-onboarding-docs.why: Building it as a reusable template with placeholders is what actually saves time on future clients, not just the current one.

fl-b2-client-onboarding-docs.q: Which is a common mistake this lesson calls out?
options: Listing exactly what you need from the client before starting
Adding a note on how fast you typically respond
Saving the documents as reusable templates
Making the packet too long, when a new client is more likely to read a short, specific one
fl-b2-client-onboarding-docs.why: The lesson explicitly warns that a packet that's too long is less likely to actually be read than a short, specific one.

fl-i1-scope-quote-contract-drafts.q: The prompt explicitly states the AI is 'not a lawyer' and instructs it to flag certain clauses. What should you do with those flagged clauses before signing?
options: Have them reviewed by a qualified professional or checked against a trusted template — they are not the finish line
Sign immediately since the AI already drafted reasonable language
Delete them since they're too risky to include
Ask the AI to make them more binding
fl-i1-scope-quote-contract-drafts.why: The lesson stresses this produces a starting point for sensitive clauses, not a finished one — professional review is required before anything is signed.

fl-i1-scope-quote-contract-drafts.q: Why should the quote be itemized into line items instead of a single lump sum?
options: Itemized quotes are legally required
It's easier for the client to see, and agree to, what they're actually paying for
It reduces the total price
It hides the total cost from the client
fl-i1-scope-quote-contract-drafts.why: An itemized quote lets the client see exactly what they're paying for, which is easier to agree to than a single lump-sum figure.

fl-i1-scope-quote-contract-drafts.q: Which of these is a mistake this lesson specifically warns against?
options: Sending the scope and quote for written approval before the contract
Using only the payment terms you actually offer
Sending an AI-drafted contract straight to a client for signature without professional review of IP, liability, or termination clauses
Itemizing the quote by deliverable
fl-i1-scope-quote-contract-drafts.why: The lesson explicitly warns against sending an AI-drafted contract for signature without professional review of legally sensitive clauses.

fl-i2-marketing-yourself-portfolio-outre.q: You didn't get a hard metric confirmed for a past project. What should the case study prompt do?
options: Estimate a plausible-sounding percentage to make the case study stronger
Skip that project entirely
Ask the client to confirm a number before writing anything
Describe the qualitative outcome honestly instead of inventing a number
fl-i2-marketing-yourself-portfolio-outre.why: The prompt explicitly instructs not to invent a metric if none was given, describing the qualitative outcome honestly instead.

fl-i2-marketing-yourself-portfolio-outre.q: Why does the outreach message reference only one relevant result from the case study, not the whole thing?
options: It produces a sharper, more targeted message than trying to summarize your entire career in three sentences
Longer messages are penalized by email spam filters
The case study format only allows one result
It's required by cold outreach best practices
fl-i2-marketing-yourself-portfolio-outre.why: Referencing one relevant result produces a sharper message than trying to cram an entire career summary into a short cold outreach note.

fl-i2-marketing-yourself-portfolio-outre.q: Which mistake most commonly makes a cold outreach message read as templated, even if the copy is well-written?
options: Using a real project as the case study source
Sending it without a genuinely personalized opening line explaining the specific reason for reaching out
Ending with a low-pressure next step
Targeting one specific client type
fl-i2-marketing-yourself-portfolio-outre.why: A missing personalized opening line is called out as the single biggest tell that a cold message wasn't actually personalized.

fl-i3-client-updates-difficult-conversat.q: Before drafting a rate-increase message, what does the lesson say you must decide first?
options: The exact word count of the final message
Which AI tool to use
Your actual position — the boundary, ask, or decision — since only you should make that business call
The client's likely emotional reaction
fl-i3-client-updates-difficult-conversat.why: Deciding your actual position before drafting keeps the real business decision — what you're conceding or holding firm on — in your hands, not the AI's.

fl-i3-client-updates-difficult-conversat.q: Why does the prompt explicitly instruct against over-apologizing in a scope-pushback message?
options: Apologies are considered legally binding admissions
It makes the message too long to read
Clients prefer messages with zero emotional language
Piling on apologetic language can actually weaken your position by making it read like you're not confident in your own ask
fl-i3-client-updates-difficult-conversat.why: Over-apologizing is a specific failure mode the lesson targets, since it weakens your position by suggesting you're not confident in your own ask.

fl-i3-client-updates-difficult-conversat.q: What should a difficult-conversation message end with, according to the prompt's rules?
options: A clear next step or specific ask, not a vague 'let me know your thoughts'
A long list of alternative options for the client to choose from
An open-ended apology
A summary of the entire project history
fl-i3-client-updates-difficult-conversat.why: Ending with a specific next step, rather than an open-ended question, is what moves the conversation forward instead of leaving the client unsure.

fl-a1-productize-your-service.q: When building standing instructions for a reusable AI project, what's the core design decision the lesson emphasizes?
options: Choosing between Claude Projects and Custom GPTs
Separating the reusable pattern (your repeatable process) from what must be custom per client every time
Deciding how many words the deliverable should be
Picking a price for the productized offer first
fl-a1-productize-your-service.why: Getting the split between reusable pattern and required customization right is the core decision — get it wrong and you either save nothing or lose the client-specific quality.

fl-a1-productize-your-service.q: Why does the prompt instruct the assistant to ask for missing checklist items rather than filling them in generically?
options: It speeds up the process
Checklists are required by Claude Projects
It prevents the system from quietly producing lower-quality work when you forget to paste in client-specific context
It reduces the number of client questions
fl-a1-productize-your-service.why: This guardrail prevents the system from silently degrading into generic output whenever a piece of client-specific context is missing.

fl-a1-productize-your-service.q: How should you determine the price for a fixed-scope productized version of your service, according to the lesson?
options: Match whatever your closest competitor charges
Use the AI's suggested price from the draft
Set it based on how long the first draft took only
Time yourself running the workflow on 2-3 real projects and use that real measured time cost, not a guess
fl-a1-productize-your-service.why: The lesson recommends pricing off real measured time across a few actual runs, not a guess, to define a fixed-scope offer.
